meta.home: I'm Lorenzo. I build custom software for businesses: tools for the work your team does every day, automation for the repetitive parts, and products built from nothing. You bring the problem.
meta.work: Selected work. For each one: what was wrong, what I built, and the part that turned out to be difficult.
meta.about: How I approach a problem that arrives without a spec, what working with me looks like, and what I've built.

hero.status: Open to a couple of projects
hero.lede: I'm Lorenzo. Businesses bring me the part of the work that's slow, repetitive or held together by a spreadsheet, and I build the thing that replaces it. Working out what should be built is usually the hard part, so that's where I start.

facts.latestValue: AInterest, an app anyone can use

capabilities.title: Most people arrive with a problem, not a plan.
capabilities.lede: Usually it's something slow, repetitive, or living in a spreadsheet nobody quite trusts. Turning that into something worth building is most of the job. And if you're not sure software is the answer at all, that's a fine place to start — working that out is part of the work.

manualWork.title: Work your team still does by hand
manualWork.body: The report someone rebuilds every Monday. Numbers moved from one system into another. Anything repetitive enough that people have stopped reading it properly. That part can be handled for you, and the hours go back to the team.

customTool.title: The tool you wish existed
customTool.body: Every business has a way of working that no off-the-shelf product quite fits, so it ends up spread across spreadsheets, shared inboxes and someone's memory. This is the thing built around how you actually operate, instead of you bending to fit the software.

ideaToProduct.title: An idea that needs to become a product
ideaToProduct.body: Something real people can sign up for and use, not a deck describing it. I've taken my own product from an idea to a live app with accounts and paying attention to the details, so you can go and click around the result.

systemsTalking.title: Tools that don't talk to each other
systemsTalking.body: The accounting system, the CRM, a supplier's portal, an old database nobody wants to touch. Getting information to move between them on its own, reliably enough that people stop double-checking it by hand.

aiWhereItPays.title: AI where it genuinely saves time
aiWhereItPays.body: I've put AI features in front of real users and recorded a course on working with these tools. That's also why I'll tell you when it's an expensive answer to something a simpler build solves better.

outgrown.title: Something you've outgrown
outgrown.body: It still works, but every small change takes weeks, everyone has a workaround, and nobody wants to touch it. Sometimes that's worth repairing and sometimes it's worth replacing. I'll tell you which, and why.

work.title: Things I've built.
work.lede: What the problem was, and what changed once the thing existed.
work.pageLede: Products, client work, and a couple of things built at hackathon speed. For each one: what was wrong, what I built, and the part that turned out to be difficult.

archive.title: Everything else.
archive.lede: Smaller builds, hackathon entries and old experiments. Most of them aren't maintained. They're here because this is the honest version of the list.

ainterest.summary: An AI image app strangers can sign up for and use.
ainterest.problem: Tools that generate images bury everything in a chat log. Whatever you made last week is effectively gone, and you never see what anyone else is doing with the same tool.
ainterest.built: You describe what you want, you get an image back, and you can publish it to a feed anyone can browse. Accounts, saved work, a shared feed — a product people can use, not a demo.
ainterest.challenge: Almost none of the difficulty was the AI itself. Generating an image is slow, it costs real money every single time, and it fails in ways ordinary software doesn't. The app has to be honest about all of that without ever looking broken, and stay quick as the feed fills up.
ainterest.value: Anyone can talk about adding AI to a product. Building one that strangers can sign up for, use and come back to is the part that counts, so that's the one I built.

nextremum.summary: A telecoms provider that had to be understood before anyone would call.
nextremum.problem: Nextremum sells private networks and connectivity across Europe and Asia. It's a considered purchase with a lot of trust attached, and nobody starts that conversation before they understand what's actually on offer.
nextremum.built: A site organised around what they sell and where they cover, structured so the offer can keep growing without a rebuild, and readable on a phone in a taxi.
nextremum.challenge: The subject is dense. It had to be quick to scan for the person signing off the budget without losing the detail the specialist on the call is checking for. Two very different readers, one page.
nextremum.value: The offer holds up whether the person reading it is buying it or specifying it.

kraanveld.summary: A crane rental company, presented like someone you'd trust with a crane.
kraanveld.problem: Renting heavy equipment is a trust decision. Before anyone picks up the phone they want to see the fleet, what's been lifted before, and that this clearly isn't the first job.
kraanveld.built: The fleet, completed work and contact details, built around large photography, and built to be updated for years rather than replaced in two.
kraanveld.challenge: The work is visual, so the site leans on big images. Those have to appear immediately on a phone, on a site with bad signal — not just on a fast office connection. That's where most of the engineering went.
kraanveld.value: Whatever makes someone pick up the phone is the first thing they see.

aiForFrontend.summary: An online course on getting real value out of AI tools.
aiForFrontend.problem: Teams were adopting AI tools without ever agreeing on where they help and where they quietly cost an afternoon.
aiForFrontend.built: I designed and recorded the whole course: what to cover, the worked examples, the delivery.
aiForFrontend.challenge: These tools change every few months. The material had to be about how you work, so it wouldn't expire alongside whichever tool happened to be ahead that month.
aiForFrontend.value: Explaining something well enough to teach it is a stricter test than being good at it yourself.

wayport.summary: Indoor airport navigation, designed and built in a weekend.
wayport.problem: Airports are hard to read when you're late. Gates, services and facilities are exactly what you can't find at the moment you need them.
wayport.built: A phone app for finding your way around inside an airport. Designed, built and demoed inside a hackathon.
wayport.challenge: Deciding what to cut. With a fixed deadline, the only way to end up with something real is to pick the one thing that has to work and drop everything else.
wayport.value: That's the same judgement a first version needs. Pick what proves the idea, and build that part properly.

archiveItems.cahulConnect: A city platform pulling local businesses, events and public services into one place. Built at GigaHack.
archiveItems.weather: Weather where you are, or the forecast for any city you look up.
archiveItems.pulse: A sports store template, built to get the layout fundamentals right.
archiveItems.writerWorks: A template built mostly as an excuse to work on animation and layout.

process.title: You talk to the person building it.
process.lede: Small engagements, no account manager in the middle.

understand.title: Work out the real problem
understand.body: A call and a lot of questions about how the work gets done today. Fairly often the thing worth building isn't the thing that was asked for, and it's much cheaper to find that out now.

scope.title: Agree the smallest useful version
scope.body: What ships first, what it costs, what's deliberately left out. A scope and a number before anything starts, not an open-ended discovery phase billed by the hour.

build.title: Build it where you can see it
build.body: You get something you can click through while it's still being built. Changing your mind is cheap early and expensive late, so I'd much rather hear it early.

handOver.title: Ship it and hand it over
handOver.body: Live, documented and yours. You shouldn't need me on a monthly retainer just to keep it running.

aboutTeaser.title: One person, start to finish.
aboutTeaser.body1: I'm Lorenzo. A software engineer, currently senior on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>, with a small number of client projects alongside it. I'm also finishing a master's at the University of Oradea.
aboutTeaser.body2: I've spent years building things end to end: the part people use every day, the part running quietly behind it, and the decisions in between. Which tools that involves is my problem to solve, not something you should have to have an opinion about.
aboutTeaser.body3: In practice it means one person holds the whole thing, from the first conversation about what's going wrong to the version your team opens on a Monday morning.

contact.title: Tell me what isn't working.
contact.lede: You don't need a spec, a budget or a plan. A few sentences about what's slow, repetitive or annoying is enough. I'll tell you honestly whether it's worth building, and whether I'm the right person to build it.

about.title: The longer version.
about.lede: Software engineer. Currently senior, still mostly curious.
about.intro: I'm Lorenzo, a software engineer and a master's student at the University of Oradea. Day to day I'm a senior engineer on <barca>Barça Mobile</barca>.
about.freelance: Alongside that I take a small number of client projects and keep my own things running. That's where I try ideas out before they end up in anyone else's business.
about.career: Most of what I've built has ended up in front of real people, which is a useful discipline: it becomes obvious very quickly when something is confusing or slow. I've also owned the parts nobody sees — how information is structured, how systems pass work between each other, and what happens on the day something fails.
about.interests: The part I actually enjoy comes before any of that: sitting with a problem until it's clear what should exist. Plenty of people can build what you describe. Fewer will tell you that what you described isn't quite what you need.

principles.title: A few things I believe about building software.

problem.title: The brief is a guess
problem.body: People describe solutions, because that's the vocabulary they have. My first job is finding the problem underneath and checking whether the thing you asked for actually solves it.

smallest.title: Ship the smallest real thing
smallest.body: A narrow version people are using teaches you more than a broad version in a document. Starting small isn't caution — it's how you avoid paying for the wrong thing twice.

maintainable.title: Someone has to live with this
maintainable.body: Whatever I build has to make sense to whoever picks it up next, including you. Clever is a liability. Boring and predictable ages far better.

ai.title: AI is a tool, not a plan
ai.body: I use these tools every day and recorded a course on them. That's exactly why I'll say it when the answer to your problem isn't AI at all.

working.title: What working with me usually looks like.
working.intro: Most of what people want to know before a first conversation is some version of these.

noSpec.label: No spec yet
noSpec.body: Normal. Almost nobody has one. A description of what's slow or annoying is a better starting point than a document written to guess at a solution.

notSure.label: Not sure it's software
notSure.body: Sometimes it isn't, and I'll say so. A change to the process, or a setting in something you already pay for, beats a build you'd have to live with.

tooSmall.label: It feels too small
tooSmall.body: A week of work that removes something your team does every single day is a good project. I'd rather do that than a six-month plan nobody finishes.

existing.label: Something already exists
existing.body: I can take over what's there, finish what stalled, or work next to whoever built it. Starting again from scratch is a decision, not a default.

money.label: Cost and timing
money.body: You get a scope and a number before anything starts, and you hear from me early if either is going to move. No surprises at the end.

outro.title: Away from the screen.
outro.body: I read more industry newsletters than is reasonable, and spend a fair amount of time on creative coding, which has no business case whatsoever. That's mostly the appeal.
